content: Chronic bronchitis is characterized by inflammation of the bronchi, which are medium-sized airways in the lungs. Unlike acute bronchitis, chronic bronchitis is not always caused by infection and is typically a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Clinically, it is defined as a persistent cough that produces sputum (phlegm) and mucus for at least three months in two consecutive years. Smoking is the most significant risk factor for developing chronic bronchitis. If left untreated, the condition can progress to a debilitating disease. The primary medical treatments include inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids. Smoking cessation and reducing exposure to environmental pollutants are effective strategies to slow disease progression and reduce mortality. The condition was first described by Charles Badham in 1808, and René Laennec later categorized COPD into emphysema and chronic bronchitis. Pathologically, chronic bronchitis is marked by hyperplasia and hypertrophy of goblet cells (mucous glands) in the airway. Chronic inflammation, often due to lymphocyte infiltration, is evident under microscopic examination. Histopathological analysis reveals infiltration of airway walls by inflammatory cells, particularly CD8+ T-lymphocytes and neutrophils. This inflammation leads to scarring and remodeling, which thickens the airway walls and narrows the small airways. Chronic bronchitis, as a subtype of COPD, arises from a combination of environmental and genetic factors. Smoking is the leading cause, but other contributors include air pollutants, occupational exposure to dust and coal, and autoimmune diseases. It is essential to differentiate chronic bronchitis from other causes of chronic cough and dyspnea, such as congestive heart failure, chronic asthma, bronchiectasis, and bronchiolitis obliterans. Epidemiologically, COPD affects approximately 34 out of 1,000 individuals over the age of 65, with an estimated 25 million cases in the U.S. when undiagnosed cases are included. Mortality rates are higher among Caucasians compared to African Americans or other racial groups. Between 1999 and 2014, age-adjusted death rates decreased among men but remained stable among women. Risk factors for chronic bronchitis include cigarette smoking, air pollution, genetic predisposition, increasing age, male gender, allergies, and repeated airway infections. Routine screening is not recommended for asymptomatic adults, as decreases in lung capacity without symptoms do not require treatment. The prognosis of chronic bronchitis depends on the timing of diagnosis and the severity of airflow obstruction, which can be measured using FEV1, FVC, or FEV1/FVC ratios. The disease spectrum ranges from well-controlled cases to severe airway obstruction with frequent exacerbations requiring hospitalization. Untreated COPD can lead to progressive deterioration and death. Common complications include recurrent pneumonia, depression, cor pulmonale, anemia, and polycythemia. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment improve outcomes, with most patients experiencing better lung function after initiating therapy. The clinical diagnosis of chronic bronchitis is based on a persistent productive cough lasting at least three months in two consecutive years. Symptoms include sputum production, shortness of breath (dyspnea), and wheezing. Occasionally, patients may also experience chest pain, fever, fatigue, or malaise. Dyspnea, often described as a sensation of air hunger or gasping for air, is a hallmark symptom. Physical examination findings in chronic bronchitis can include cyanosis, tachypnea, use of accessory respiratory muscles, paradoxical inward movement of the lower intercostal spaces (Hoover sign), elevated jugular venous pressure, and peripheral edema. Pulmonary examination may reveal a barrel chest (in cases of emphysema), wheezing, hyperresonance, crackles, and rhonchi. These signs are more apparent in severe disease and may be difficult to detect in mild to moderate cases. Laboratory findings in chronic bronchitis include irreversible airflow limitation, particularly during forced expiration, due to lung tissue destruction and increased airway resistance. Unlike asthma, FEV1 does not improve after bronchodilator administration. COPD is diagnosed via spirometry when the FEV1/FVC ratio is less than 70%. Arterial blood gas analysis may reveal hypoxemia with or without hypercapnia, depending on disease severity. Renal compensation may normalize pH levels, but a pH below 7.3 indicates severe respiratory compromise. Reactive polycythemia, a response to chronic hypoxemia, may be observed in venous blood samples. Electrocardiographic findings in chronic bronchitis include P pulmonale, right ventricular strain, right ventricular hypertrophy, and an S1S2S3 pattern. Chest X-rays are not routinely recommended for diagnosis but are often ordered to exclude other causes of dyspnea and productive cough, such as pneumonia or heart failure. Common radiographic findings in chronic bronchitis include hyperinflation and hyperlucency of the lungs. CT scans are not typically required but can help rule out other causes of chronic cough and dyspnea. Echocardiography is useful for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension in patients with long-standing chronic bronchitis. The primary goal of treatment is to improve lung function and slow the decline in pulmonary capacity. Treatment strategies focus on two main objectives: reducing symptoms (e.g., relieving dyspnea and improving exercise tolerance) and reducing risks (e.g., treating exacerbations, preventing disease progression, and lowering mortality). Inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids are the cornerstone of medical therapy. Smoking cessation, controlling air pollutants, and minimizing occupational exposure to dust and fumes are critical preventive measures. Secondary prevention also emphasizes smoking cessation and reducing occupational exposures to decrease morbidity and mortality.
